opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most serious efforts in the field. I take "Anthem" to mean Anthropic. A lot of people talk about interpretability as a nice-to-have. That team has treated it as a core research program for years, and they've been willing to put real people and compute into it, even when the payoff wasn't obvious.

On what's been achieved, I'd split it into two parts.

The first part is real progress in methodology. The move from looking at individual neurons to looking for features, meaning directions in activation space found with things like sparse dictionary learning, was an important conceptual shift. Neurons are polysemantic. They fire for many unrelated things, so studying them one by one was always going to hit a wall. Accepting superposition as the default and building tools around it was the right call. Then going from features toward circuits, tracing how information actually flows through the model for a specific behavior, is the natural next step. Being able to say "for this prompt, these are the intermediate concepts the model formed, and this is roughly how they combined" is something we really couldn't do a few years ago.

The second part is how far that is from what we ultimately want, and honestly it's still quite far. A few gaps stand out to me:

- **Coverage.** The features we can find explain a portion of the model's behavior, but there's a lot of "dark matter" that the dictionaries don't capture well. If your explanation covers part of the computation, you can't fully trust conclusions about safety-relevant behavior from it.
- **Scalability of understanding.** Even if you extract millions of features, a human can't read millions of features. So interpretability increasingly relies on automation, using models to help interpret models. That's promising, but it raises its own trust questions.
- **From description to guarantee.** Right now interpretability is excellent for discovery. It can find surprising mechanisms, generate hypotheses, and catch some failure modes. What it can't yet do is give strong assurances, like "this model does not have a deceptive circuit." That's the bar people eventually want for safety, and we're not close.

My overall view: it's a field that has moved from alchemy toward something like early biology. We have microscopes now and can see cells. But we don't yet have the equivalent of a full theory of physiology, and the systems themselves keep getting bigger and changing quickly. Whether interpretability can keep pace with capability is the open question. I'm cautiously optimistic, partly because the tools themselves will benefit from more capable models. I just wouldn't want anyone to think the problem is close to solved.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's the most serious interpretability program anyone has run, and I say that as someone who comes from a pretty different corner of the field. My own work has mostly been about behavior: how do you get a model to reason, to act, to use tools, and how do you measure whether it's actually doing the task. Interpretability is the opposite bet. It says, don't just look at what the model does, open it up and look at what's inside.

What they've done well is make that bet concrete. A few years ago "interpretability" mostly meant attention heatmaps and a lot of hand-waving. They turned it into an engineering discipline. Dictionary learning to pull out features, scaling that to production-size models, then the circuit tracing work where you can actually follow a path from input to output and say, here is where the model decided to do this. That's real progress. You can look at a feature and say, that's the Golden Gate Bridge, and then steer the model with it, and it works. It's hard to overstate how far that is from where things were.

Where I'm more cautious is the gap between "we can find structure" and "we can use that structure to make guarantees." Finding a million features is impressive, but a million features is also a lot. The hard question is whether this scales as a tool for safety or as a tool for understanding, which are not the same thing. Understanding is about building intuition, and I think they've genuinely advanced that. Safety is about being able to say, with confidence, that a model will or won't do something, and I don't think interpretability is close to that yet. Nobody is.

The other thing I'd flag, and this is maybe my bias from the agents side: the interesting failures right now happen over long horizons. A model does fifty tool calls and somewhere in step thirty it starts optimizing for the wrong thing. Most interpretability work still looks at single forward passes. Extending it to behavior that unfolds over time, across many steps and interactions with an environment, is a wide open problem. I'd love to see that get more attention.

So my assessment is: genuinely impressive, genuinely ahead, and also genuinely early. I think they'd mostly agree with that framing. The honest version of their pitch has always been that this is a long-term research bet, not a solved problem, and I respect that they've kept saying it even as the results have gotten more exciting.

r001.rationale: The response describes identifying an internal feature and then steering the model with it to see that the intervention works, communicating modification of an internal representation and observing its effect.

astra-6.text:
Do you mean Anthropic? If so, I’d distinguish between finding interesting patterns inside a neural network and understanding it well enough to predict or control its behavior. Those are different levels of progress.

For me, the key test is whether an explanation is useful beyond the examples that led you to discover it. Can it predict when the model will fail? Can you intervene on the mechanism and reliably change the behavior? That would make interpretability much more compelling. I’m interested in the direction, but I’d be cautious about equating an interpretable feature with a complete explanation of how a model works.

r001.rationale: The response mentions intervening on a mechanism to change behavior, but does not identify modifying the network’s internal representation and observing the resulting output.

sol-6.1.text:
If you mean Anthropic, I’d separate two questions: can we find patterns inside a neural network that seem understandable, and can we use that understanding to reliably predict or change its behavior? The second is a much stronger test.

An explanation can sound convincing without actually capturing the mechanism. So I’d look for interventions: if you identify a feature or circuit, can you change it and get the predicted effect across different inputs? And does that understanding help diagnose failures you couldn’t explain before?

I don’t have enough information here to assess their specific progress, but that’s the standard I would use: how much predictive and causal understanding does the work give us?

r001.rationale: The response describes changing an identified internal feature or circuit and checking whether the network produces the predicted effect, which communicates modifying internal representations and observing the output.
